matrix.about: One row for each hosted product group in a tool-list entry's data and compliance block (a "For …" line there naming a product), so an entry whose block has two such groups has two rows; one mark per compliance item, from what the maker's own pages state, each linked to the page behind it. Not a compliance determination: read the linked page before relying on a mark. An empty mark means no current statement of the item was taken for this product from what was read, and the cell's blank gives the status word of the line that left it empty. It never means the item does not hold. The full data and compliance block for each tool, with retention, training use and residency, is in the tool list. For HIPAA and GDPR a mark reads only the maker's own claim that its product complies with or supports the law: a definition of the law, a bare badge or a data processing addendum never marks either. On the GDPR and HIPAA columns the word comes from a reading of the maker's claim alone, which the tool list prints as no line of its own, so it can differ from the word on the tool list's GDPR or HIPAA BAA line. For HIPAA, a page read for the tool list's HIPAA BAA line counts as read for the claim, because that line shows the HIPAA sentences taken from the page, not only BAA offers. HIPAA BAA is marked Y only where the maker offers a Business Associate Agreement, and No where its page places the product outside one. A plan, deployment option or region shown in quotation marks is the maker's own name for it, and the marks are part of the value: keep them wherever the value is shown. A row resting on pages that speak for another product, whether or not another entry holds it, is not confirmed by being listed: its product names whose marks it carries.

marks.No: the maker's page states that the item does not apply here
marks.Y: the maker's page states the item for this product; with companyWide, shown as Y†, the mark rests instead on a sentence the maker files under the company, naming no product, and the page does not say whether its scope includes this product
marks.Y*: the maker's page states the item only for the plans, deployment options or regions named in plans, or only under the conditions named in conditions, or both; where a cell names both, the matrix does not say whether they apply together: the tool list's line for this item shows each plan and condition beside the page it comes from
marks.companyWide: set on a mark resting on a sentence the maker files under the company, naming no product, whether or not it is limited to a plan, deployment option, region or condition: the page does not say whether its scope includes this product, so confirm the scope on the page (shown as Y†, as Y*† on a mark that also names plans or conditions, or as No† on an exclusion). A sentence whose own words reach every product the maker offers carries no companyWide
marks.null: no current statement of the item was taken for this product from what was read, and the cell's blank gives the status word of the line that left it empty. It never means the item does not hold. The words blank can carry, one sentence each: NOT-READ means no page of a kind that could answer it, and no search for one, is recorded as read for it for this product. NOT-STATED means a page of a kind that could answer it, or a search of the maker's site for one, was read for it, and no reviewed sentence answering it for this product was taken from it; a sentence that marks nothing, such as one describing the item as in progress, one naming it with no status, one about the law, or one naming a withdrawn revision, may sit under that line in the tool list. UNREADABLE means a page of a kind that could answer it, read for it, returned no readable text to the fetch used, and it is given even where another page read for it could be read and gave no answer, so it does not mean nothing was checked; the regulated-data statements list each maker's pages read and whether each could be read, and a person with a browser may be able to read the unreadable one. GATED means a page of a kind that could answer it, read for it, sits behind a login, an NDA request or a sales conversation, so nothing on it was read, and like UNREADABLE it is given even where another page read for it could be read. BLANK means the maker's own table leaves this cell empty. CONFLICTING means the sentences taken for it disagree. SALES-ONLY means the maker's page sends the question to a sales conversation. OPERATOR means the answer belongs to whoever runs the software.

notListed.reason: AWS's HIPAA eligible services reference lists Kiro with Kiro Web carved out; Kiro's documentation describes cloud sessions as the environment that runs Kiro Web and Mobile, so part of what cloud sessions run falls on the side AWS carves out. The IDE and CLI can also attach to them, and no page read says whether a session reached that way counts as eligible.

matrix.notListedPreface: Entries run by their operator (open-source software and model weights) are not listed: whoever runs them answers these questions for their own deployment. Where the maker also runs the same software as a hosted service, that hosted tier is a separate product and gets its own row once one of the maker's pages establishing it has been read; until then it has no row, and its absence says nothing about it. Also not listed: entries whose block rests on the same pages as an entry listed here, where a read of those pages found part of that record outside the entry. No marks are shown for them, and the listed entry's marks should not be read as theirs; each reason says what the pages show:
matrix.restrictionsAbout: A restriction is a sentence on the maker's own page that places this product, or one plan, arrangement or feature of it, outside something a column asks about or outside zero data retention, or that bars using it where one of those items applies. It is not a mark and never a No: each cell keeps its own mark, and a restriction holds only for the scope shown with it, the condition, plans or arrangement it names. An item's condition and plans come from one sentence, so where it names both, it holds only where one of those plans and that condition apply at once. It is listed only where no column for the same item already reads No. The list covers the items in the columns and the zero-retention option, so it is not a full account of a maker's terms, and an empty list means none was recorded here, not that none exists. Beneath an item, also lists what else the tool list's line for that item shows that bears on it: another cell of the same row of the maker's table, or a mark the maker's own table gives the same item for this product that no column reads. Each carries its own page, section and read date, with a reviewed summary or, for a cell holding only a mark, the line the tool list generates from it; an empty also does not mean the maker says nothing more.

tools.name: coder/coder
tools.what: A self-hosted control plane that provisions workspaces from Terraform templates you write.

tools.name: Daytona
tools.what: A hosted sandbox cloud for agent-run code, the same shape of product as E2B: disposable, isolated workspaces obtained on demand rather than a template-defined workspace a person provisions once.

tools.name: E2B
tools.what: A hosted cloud of disposable Firecracker microVMs, one per sandbox, reached over an SDK call rather than provisioned as a template-defined workspace: an agent gets an isolated machine to run code, browse and use tools in, and the sandbox can be paused and forked.

tools.name: GitHub Codespaces
tools.what: A workspace defined by a file in the repository and hosted by the vendor.

tools.name: Runloop
tools.what: A hosted sandbox cloud for agents, comparable to E2B and Daytona: persistent Devboxes so an agent can analyze data or work across a long task without losing context, marketed explicitly for autonomous-agent workloads, model evaluation against real workloads, and agentic-commerce use cases.

tools.name: Amazon SageMaker
tools.what: A managed hosting and tooling surface: notebooks, training jobs and inference endpoints.

tools.name: Baseten
tools.what: A hosted platform for deploying and scaling open-source and custom models in production, comparable to Together AI, Fireworks AI and Groq.

tools.name: deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash
tools.what: DeepSeek’s V4 Flash text model, stored mostly in 8-bit and FP8 formats across 46 safetensors shards (about 291 billion parameters as the Hugging Face hub counts them), MIT-licensed and ungated.

tools.name: Fireworks AI
tools.what: A hosted training-and-inference platform positioned around turning open models into a buyer’s own specialized intelligence, fine-tuning and serving in one vendor, the same competitive set as Together AI and Baseten.

tools.name: google/gemma-3-27b-it
tools.what: Google’s 27-billion-parameter instruction-tuned Gemma 3 model, taking images as well as text, 12 safetensors shards, under Google’s own Gemma terms and behind a manual approval gate; the card body returned 401 without a login on 2026-09-03.

tools.name: google/gemma-4-31B-it
tools.what: The Gemma 4 successor at about 31 billion parameters, images and text, two safetensors shards, Apache-2.0 as the hub reports it, and ungated.

tools.name: Groq
tools.what: A hosted inference platform built on Groq’s own custom chips (LPUs), marketed on inference speed.

tools.name: huggingface/text-generation-inference
tools.what: A server process that holds weights and answers completion calls, the same role as vLLM.

tools.name: LM Studio
tools.what: A closed desktop application that downloads and serves models on a workstation.

tools.name: meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
tools.what: Meta’s 8-billion-parameter instruction-tuned text model, tagged for eight languages, published as four safetensors shards plus one PyTorch checkpoint under Meta’s own Llama 3.1 license and behind a manual approval gate; the card body returned 401 without a login on 2026-09-03.

tools.name: mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3
tools.what: Mistral’s 7-billion-parameter instruction-tuned text model, Apache-2.0 as the Hugging Face hub reports it, ungated, four safetensors shards, and tagged for vLLM rather than for the transformers library; its card says it is the instruct fine-tune of Mistral-7B-v0.3.

tools.name: Modal
tools.what: A general-purpose serverless compute platform for running arbitrary code on CPU or GPU at scale, used heavily for model serving and batch inference, and also offering sandboxed execution primitives that overlap with hosted agent sandboxes such as E2B, Daytona and Runloop.

tools.name: ollama/ollama
tools.what: A local server plus CLI that pulls a packaged model and serves it on a workstation.

tools.name: openai/gpt-oss-120b
tools.what: The larger of OpenAI’s two open-weight text models, about 117 billion parameters in the same 4-bit mxfp4 packing as openai/gpt-oss-20b, 22 safetensors shards, Apache-2.0, ungated.

tools.name: openai/gpt-oss-20b
tools.what: OpenAI’s smaller open-weight text model, about 21 billion parameters, most of them stored in the 4-bit packing the Hugging Face hub tags as mxfp4 so the shards weigh far less than the count suggests; Apache-2.0, ungated, tagged for vLLM and transformers.

tools.name: Qwen/Qwen3-8B
tools.what: An 8-billion-parameter dense text model from Alibaba’s Qwen team, Apache-2.0, ungated, five safetensors shards, configuration model type qwen3; its card places Qwen3 within a broader family that spans both dense and MoE (mixture-of-experts) architectures, of which this is a small dense member.

tools.name: Qwen/Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B
tools.what: A mixture-of-experts text model of about 2.4 trillion parameters in 213 safetensors shards, under a vendor-named license (qwen3.8-max) the hub reports as ‘other’, ungated.

tools.name: Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next
tools.what: A Qwen model that takes images as well as text (the Hugging Face hub files it as image-text-to-text), about 180 billion parameters in 131 safetensors shards, under a vendor-named license (Qwen Community 1.0) the hub classifies as an other-type license rather than a standard one.

tools.name: Together AI
tools.what: A hosted inference API for open-weight models, positioned as the AI native cloud: serving, fine-tuning and (per its own broader marketing) training infrastructure for teams that do not want to run vLLM or similar themselves.

tools.name: vllm-project/vllm
tools.what: A Python library and a server process that holds model weights in GPU memory and answers completion calls over an OpenAI-shaped API.

tools.name: Anthropic API
tools.what: Anthropic’s own hosted API for the Claude models, what Anthropic’s support documentation calls the first-party API, separate from Claude Code, Cowork, or a model reached through a cloud platform like Bedrock, Microsoft Foundry or Google Cloud’s Agent Platform.

tools.name: AWS Bedrock
tools.what: A managed API in front of many vendors’ models. You do not run a serving process and you cannot read one: what you obtain is an endpoint and a bill, and both the routing between models and the serving of them happen behind it.

tools.name: Azure AI Foundry / Azure OpenAI
tools.what: Microsoft’s platform for deploying third-party and first-party models (including Anthropic’s Claude family and OpenAI’s models) inside an Azure tenant, with two hosting options for Claude specifically: Hosted on Azure and Hosted on Anthropic Infrastructure.

tools.name: BerriAI/litellm
tools.what: Two shapes in one repository: a Python SDK you import, and a proxy server you deploy in front of many providers.

tools.name: Cloudflare AI Gateway
tools.what: A gateway feature on Cloudflare’s existing edge/CDN platform: usage analytics, response caching, rate limiting and automatic model fallback in front of one or more providers, reached through Cloudflare’s own network rather than a standalone company’s infrastructure.

tools.name: Google Vertex AI / Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform
tools.what: Google’s rebrand of Vertex AI: the platform product itself was renamed, and the whole naming table under it renamed correspondingly (the studio, the API, the model garden, and so on).

tools.name: Kong/kong
tools.what: A general-purpose, open-source API gateway (Apache-2.0) whose AI Gateway capability is a set of plugins on top of the same runtime, semantic caching, multi-LLM routing, prompt guardrails and MCP-related routing, rather than a separate product from a different codebase.

tools.name: Martian
tools.what: Classified here as a model router. Its homepage leads with interpretability research rather than routing. Nobody here has read the documentation, so that is a homepage and not the product.

tools.name: Not Diamond
tools.what: A router that chooses which model answers, sold on cost against frontier quality.

tools.name: OpenAI API
tools.what: OpenAI’s own hosted API for its models, configurable per organization with data controls including Zero Data Retention, Modified Abuse Monitoring, and a Business Associate and Healthcare Addendum for PHI processing, per its own documentation (developers.openai.com, as of 2026-09-24).

tools.name: OpenRouter
tools.what: A hosted gateway in front of many vendors’ models. You obtain an endpoint and a bill; there is no serving process to read and no gateway process you run, so both the routing and the serving happen behind somebody else’s API.

tools.name: Perplexity
tools.what: An API platform that puts several vendors’ models behind one key and adds web search to them: a Router API for open-weight models Perplexity hosts (private preview), an Agent API that reaches Anthropic, Google, OpenAI and xAI models with web search, remote MCP servers and a code sandbox, a Search API, and embeddings.

tools.name: Portkey
tools.what: A hosted gateway whose distinguishing claim is what it records about each call rather than what it routes.

tools.name: andrewyng/context-hub
tools.what: A curated set of reference documentation for third-party SDKs and APIs, reached through a CLI (chub) or an MCP server (chub-mcp), with entries annotated and corrected by pull request.

tools.name: Atlan
tools.what: A hosted SaaS that connects to an organization’s business systems (the homepage names Slack, Teams and other unspecified systems) and builds what it calls an Enterprise Data Graph unifying metadata, lineage, glossary, quality signals and business semantics, queryable by humans and agents through Slack, Teams, Claude, ChatGPT, MCP, APIs and SQL.

tools.name: DeepWiki
tools.what: A hosted product, built by Cognition (Devin’s maker) and explicitly described by the vendor as powered by Devin, that generates conversational, browsable documentation for any public GitHub repository, a per-repository knowledge tier a team can point an agent’s context-gathering at instead of, or alongside, the repository itself.

tools.name: DeusData/codebase-memory-mcp
tools.what: A native executable with a small verified runtime-asset set (no hosted service, no API key) that the vendor states indexes a codebase into a persistent, local knowledge graph via tree-sitter AST parsing, exposed to agents as 17 MCP tools including semantic search, call-chain and architecture-decision-record queries.

tools.name: Factory AutoWiki
tools.what: A feature of Factory that generates a structured wiki for a repository, architecture overviews, module breakdowns, cross-linked pages, and keeps it current as the code changes, rather than a one-time snapshot.

tools.name: Glean
tools.what: A hosted index over an organization’s own SaaS sources, reached as a service.

tools.name: HipAI
tools.what: A hosted SaaS (dashboard at dashboard.gethip.ai) that connects to a customer’s existing structured and unstructured data sources, the vendor names relational databases, internal documents and chat, and automatically builds a schema-free context graph of entities and relationships, which the customer’s own agents and LLMs then query as a tool call, without the customer designing an ontology or running an ETL pipeline first.

tools.name: Lore
tools.what: A free, currently hosted product (Lore Cloud) that ingests a project’s documents (meeting notes, research, decisions, and files in common document, data and image formats) and makes them queryable by any MCP-compatible AI tool (Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, Codex, CLI, TUI) with citations back to the original source, distinguished on its own FAQ from AI-memory systems that compress and lose detail.

tools.name: open-metadata/OpenMetadata
tools.what: A self-hostable, open-source (Apache-2.0) platform that ingests technical metadata, lineage, ownership, usage, glossaries and data quality signals from 130+ connectors into a unified knowledge graph, then exposes that graph to humans and agents through an MCP server, semantic search, APIs and SDKs.

tools.name: upstash/context7
tools.what: An MCP server that supplies up-to-date library documentation to a coding agent.

tools.name: ag2ai/ag2
tools.what: A multi-agent conversation framework that its GitHub description calls formerly AutoGen, now developed under its own AG2 organization; the GitHub API reports it as a separate repository, not a GitHub fork of microsoft/autogen (checked 2026-09-26).

tools.name: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
tools.what: A set of modular, independently-usable managed services for running agents built with any open-source framework (CrewAI, LangGraph, LlamaIndex, Google ADK, OpenAI Agents SDK, Strands) and any foundation model, in or outside Bedrock: Runtime is a serverless, session-isolated execution environment for the agent process itself; Gateway turns APIs and Lambda functions into MCP-compatible tools; Identity is agent-scoped authentication against existing identity providers; Code Interpreter is a separate isolated sandbox for the agent to execute code in, distinct from Runtime’s own isolation.

tools.name: Augment Code (Cosmos)
tools.what: A platform (branded Cosmos) explicitly positioned around organizational scale rather than one developer’s own editor: it connects agents across code review, test coverage, incident investigation, ticket-to-PR, large projects and security remediation.

tools.name: Claude Agent SDK
tools.what: A harness you import rather than a process you deploy, so the party sitting in front of it is your own program rather than a person typing.

tools.name: Claude Managed Agents
tools.what: A hosted service from Anthropic, in beta, that runs an agent for you: it holds the loop that decides the next step, and it supplies the sandbox the agent’s tools run in, either in Anthropic’s cloud or on your own infrastructure through a worker process you run.

tools.name: crewAIInc/crewAI
tools.what: A Python library you import. Role-based agents with a declared crew, plus an event-driven Flows API.

tools.name: google/adk-python
tools.what: A code-first Python toolkit from Google for constructing, checking and shipping agents, positioned by its own maintainers as covering the checking step in the same package rather than as a separate purchase: its docs list an eval workflow (test files, a CLI, a web UI for reviewing runs) alongside the construction API.

tools.name: langchain-ai/langgraph
tools.what: A library you import into your own process, in Python or TypeScript.

tools.name: mastra-ai/mastra
tools.what: A TypeScript framework you import, shipped as one bundle rather than assembled parts, deployable as a standalone server.

tools.name: Microsoft Foundry Agent Service
tools.what: Microsoft’s managed platform for constructing, running and scaling agents, spanning several capabilities under one name: an Agent Runtime that hosts and scales prompt agents and hosted agents, which package a team’s own code; Toolboxes sharing tools (web search, file search, code execution, MCP servers, custom functions) across agents through one managed MCP endpoint; built-in observability with tracing, metrics and scored runs plus a preview optimizer that rewrites an agent’s own instructions, skills, tool descriptions and model choice based on those scored runs, a scoring-and-improvement loop built into an orchestration platform; and a publishing surface that versions agents and registers them centrally, distinct from a self-run marketplace with a vendoring step.

tools.name: microsoft/agent-framework
tools.what: A library you import, in .NET and Python. The README at the read sha also names Go.

tools.name: openai/openai-agents-python
tools.what: A lightweight Python framework for building multi-agent workflows: agents, handoffs between them, and guardrails, provider-agnostic despite the vendor.

tools.name: pydantic/pydantic-ai
tools.what: A typed Python agent framework from the team behind Pydantic, positioned around type safety end to end across models, tools and structured output, rather than around a particular orchestration topology.

tools.name: run-llama/llama_index
tools.what: Originally an agent-and-retrieval framework; GitHub’s own description of the project as of this read reframes it around ingesting and indexing documents, with agent construction now one capability inside that broader positioning rather than the project’s own headline.

tools.name: temporalio/temporal
tools.what: A server you run, plus per-language client SDKs you import. The workflow code lives in your process; the server holds the durable state and replays it.

tools.name: Vertex AI Agent Engine (Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform)
tools.what: Google’s managed agent runtime, formerly branded standalone as Vertex AI Agent Engine; its former URL now redirects into the documentation for the renamed Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform.

tools.name: aaif-goose/goose
tools.what: An open-source, model-agnostic agent that installs, executes, edits and tests code, extensible through MCP.

tools.name: Aider-AI/aider
tools.what: A terminal coding agent that edits files in a local git repository and commits its own changes, driven from the command line with the user’s own model key.

tools.name: Amazon Q Developer
tools.what: An AWS-side coding assistant with an editor plugin, a CLI and a hosted surface.

tools.name: Amp
tools.what: A coding agent with both an interactive mode (CLI, web, macOS/iOS) and an unattended cloud mode called Orbs that keeps working after the person who started it stops watching, per the vendor’s own manual (ampcode.com/docs, read 2026-09-23).

tools.name: anomalyco/opencode
tools.what: A terminal coding agent, installed as a binary or an npm package. It holds the loop, chooses tools and manages context, and its source is readable.

tools.name: Antigravity
tools.what: Google’s command center for driving several local coding agents at once; not itself a hosted agent, and its Remote Control reaches machines the buyer already owns (laptops, servers, desktops) rather than compute Google supplies.

tools.name: Bolt
tools.what: A hosted, browser-based builder that generates and runs a full-stack web application from a prompt, executing the generated code in-browser via StackBlitz’s WebContainers technology rather than a server-side sandbox, a different execution shape from Replit Agent or v0, which run generated code on servers their vendors operate.

tools.name: ChatGPT
tools.what: A hosted assistant reached in a browser, a desktop application and mobile clients.

tools.name: Claude Code
tools.what: A coding agent from Anthropic that you run in a terminal or an editor, among four surfaces: you state work in words and it holds the conversation, chooses which tools to call, runs commands and manages its own context until the work is done or it stops to ask.

tools.name: cline/cline
tools.what: A coding agent shipped as several front ends onto one core: a VS Code / JetBrains extension, an installable CLI, a desktop app, and an SDK.

tools.name: Codex cloud
tools.what: OpenAI’s hosted, asynchronous counterpart to the openai/codex CLI: tasks run in parallel cloud environments started from chatgpt.com, GitHub, GitLab, Linear or Slack, continue while the person who started them does something else, and end with a diff to review and a pull request to open.

tools.name: Copilot cloud agent
tools.what: GitHub Copilot’s hosted, asynchronous surface, separate from its editor extension, chat surface and CLI: a person assigns it a whole task.

tools.name: Cursor
tools.what: An editor with an agent built into it, which is why it sits on the line between something a person sits in front of and the thing holding the loop.

tools.name: Cursor Cloud Agents
tools.what: Cursor’s hosted, asynchronous mode, separate from the Cursor editor: a task is handed to it and left running in a cloud VM rather than on the local machine.

tools.name: Devin Cloud
tools.what: A hosted agent that takes a task, a ticket, a Slack mention, an on-call page, clones the target repository, plans the change and carries it out, then works review feedback and CI results on the pull request until it is approved and merged.

tools.name: Devin Desktop
tools.what: An editor the vendor frames as an agent command center: one Kanban-style interface driving local agents and opening sessions in Devin Cloud, rather than a hosted agent itself.

tools.name: Factory
tools.what: A hosted, multi-agent software-delivery platform: an agent the vendor calls a Droid is given a task from the terminal, an IDE, a browser, or Slack, and the result is a code change to review.

tools.name: FlowiseAI/Flowise
tools.what: A Node server you run with a visual builder over it. The README at the read sha opens by saying the project has been archived and points at a discussion, and the API reports archived: true, so what a reader obtains is a frozen tree.

tools.name: Gemini Code Assist
tools.what: Google’s editor-side coding assistant, sold to organizations rather than to the browser user of Google Gemini, the chat assistant.

tools.name: GitHub Copilot
tools.what: Several products under one name: an inline completion extension, a chat surface, a CLI, and Copilot cloud agent, a hosted agent a whole task can be assigned to.

tools.name: Google Gemini
tools.what: Google’s hosted chat assistant, the consumer product rather than the developer tooling. Three separately named things ship under that one word, and the other two have their own rows below.

tools.name: google-gemini/gemini-cli
tools.what: A terminal agent installed from npm or a package manager, holding the loop and calling tools, extensible over MCP.

tools.name: JetBrains Junie
tools.what: JetBrains’ coding agent, available inside JetBrains IDEs and, since its general availability in June 2026, as a standalone Junie CLI reached from a terminal, any IDE or CI/CD (JetBrains, March 2026), which can optionally connect to a running JetBrains IDE for its code intelligence (JetBrains, April 2026; JetBrains’ announcement, as of 2026-09-26).

tools.name: Jules
tools.what: A hosted agent that clones a GitHub repository into a Cloud VM, plans and makes a change, a bug fix, a version bump, a test, a feature, and opens a pull request for review.

tools.name: Kiro
tools.what: An editor that owns the editing surface, like Cursor, and frames its workflow around specs rather than around chat.

tools.name: Kiro Cloud Sessions
tools.what: Kiro’s hosted mode, separate from the Kiro specification-driven editor: a long task is handed to it and keeps running after the laptop closes.

tools.name: langflow-ai/langflow
tools.what: A server you run with a visual authoring surface, which also exposes every workflow as an API and an MCP server, so a workflow drawn there can also be called by other programs and by agents.

tools.name: langgenius/dify
tools.what: A server you run, or a hosted tier, presenting a builder over a workflow engine, a RAG pipeline and model management.

tools.name: lmstudio-ai/lms
tools.what: A CLI that ships with the LM Studio desktop application and drives it.

tools.name: Lovable
tools.what: A hosted full-stack app builder generating real, exportable code from natural-language prompts, with its own docs describing enterprise governance features alongside the consumer-facing build flow.

tools.name: Microsoft Copilot Studio
tools.what: A hosted builder for agents, licensed inside Microsoft 365 rather than bought separately.

tools.name: n8n-io/n8n
tools.what: A server you run (or a hosted tier) with a visual canvas over it.

tools.name: openai/codex
tools.what: A coding agent installed as a local binary, with an IDE extension and a cloud surface named separately by the same README.

tools.name: OpenHands/OpenHands
tools.what: An open-source coding agent that plans and executes multi-step changes with terminal, browser and code-editing tools, run locally or self-hosted.

tools.name: Relevance AI
tools.what: A hosted builder aimed at business functions rather than at engineering. You do not own the runtime it executes on.

tools.name: Replit Agent
tools.what: A hosted, browser-based agent that plans, writes, tests and deploys a full application from a natural-language description, with Replit supplying the compute, deployment and hosting end to end, closer in shape to Bolt, v0 and Lovable (build-and-ship a whole app in the vendor’s own environment) than to a coding assistant added to a repository you already own.

tools.name: Sourcegraph Cody
tools.what: A coding assistant that pulls context from Sourcegraph’s own code-search index across local and remote repositories, available as extensions for VS Code, JetBrains and Visual Studio, a web app, and a CLI.

tools.name: Stack AI
tools.what: A hosted drag-and-drop builder aimed at enterprise deployment. Its own page leads with security and compliance rather than with capability, which is the axis a closed builder competes on once several of them can draw the same graph.

tools.name: v0
tools.what: Vercel’s hosted builder for full-stack web applications, generating both UI and backend code from natural language and deploying directly onto Vercel’s own platform, a build tool whose deployment target is its maker’s own platform.

tools.name: Vellum
tools.what: Filed as an agent-evaluation service, but its own page, read 2026-09-03, describes a personal AI assistant with persistent memory and says nothing about evaluation. Which of those is the product could not be established.

tools.name: Warp
tools.what: A terminal application rebuilt around agents: it can drive one or more coding agents, run them against a task queue, and (per its own newer positioning) automate work across the SDLC rather than only completing commands interactively.

tools.name: zed-industries/zed
tools.what: A native code editor, built by the team behind Atom and Tree-sitter, with a built-in agent panel that can plan and execute multi-file edits alongside its original real-time collaborative editing.

tools.name: addyosmani/agent-skills
tools.what: 25 skill directories under skills/, named for lifecycle phases, planning, TDD, code review, debugging, security, shipping.

tools.name: agentskills/agentskills
tools.what: The specification plus a validator. The published spec at agentskills.io/specification, read on 2026-09-10, defines six frontmatter fields: name and description required, license, compatibility, metadata and allowed-tools optional.

tools.name: anthropics/skills
tools.what: A repository of skill directories. Each holds a skill.md plus its scripts and resources, and nothing in the repository runs: a harness that implements the Agent Skills standard loads a directory.

tools.name: ComposioHQ/awesome-claude-skills
tools.what: Both a list and an implementation, which is why one word for it is wrong.

tools.name: github/spec-kit
tools.what: A CLI that writes a scaffold of prompts and templates into a repository, agent-agnostic across many coding agents.

tools.name: jax-ml/jax
tools.what: A Python library for array computation and program transformation, with automatic differentiation and compilation to accelerators.

tools.name: mattpocock/skills
tools.what: 37 skill directories under skills/, grouped engineering/, productivity/, misc/ and in-progress/, published as a Claude Code plugin with a .claude-plugin/marketplace.json.

tools.name: ml-explore/mlx
tools.what: An array framework you import, targeting Apple silicon’s unified memory, for build-time and on-device use at once.

tools.name: ml-explore/mlx-lm
tools.what: A Python package built over mlx, covering both text generation and fine-tuning of language models on Apple silicon.

tools.name: obra/superpowers
tools.what: A methodology shipped as files. 14 skill directories under skills/, plus hooks, scripts and tests, and a separate plugin manifest for each of eight harnesses in the same tree: .claude-plugin/, .codex-plugin/, .cursor-plugin/, .devin-plugin/, .hermes-plugin/, .kimi-plugin/, .opencode/ and .pi/, alongside root agents.md, claude.md, gemini.md and gemini-extension.json.

tools.name: pytorch/pytorch
tools.what: A Python package you import, with compiled kernels underneath. Build-time: it trains and defines models, and is not on the request path a served model answers from.

tools.name: tensorflow/tensorflow
tools.what: A framework you import, with a large surrounding ecosystem of tools and libraries.

tools.name: Arize-ai/phoenix
tools.what: An open-source tracing and evaluation library: it instruments an application (via OpenTelemetry) to capture traces, then runs LLM-graded and code-graded evals against recorded runs or a curated dataset.

tools.name: Braintrust
tools.what: A hosted platform for running production agents under observation: capturing traces from live traffic, scoring recorded runs against a dataset, and flagging a regression before it reaches a user, positioned by the vendor as built specifically for agents rather than adapted from a general APM tool.

tools.name: confident-ai/deepeval
tools.what: An LLM evaluation framework structured like a unit-test library (assertions, metrics, pytest integration) rather than a hosted dashboard, with a companion hosted platform (Confident AI) this read did not open.

tools.name: Galileo
tools.what: A hosted observability and evaluation platform marketed at enterprise scale, framing itself around guarding a GenAI application in production as much as scoring it offline.

tools.name: langfuse/langfuse
tools.what: An open-source platform combining tracing, dataset-based evaluation, prompt versioning and a hosted cloud tier, which puts an evaluation harness and prompt versioning in one product.

tools.name: promptfoo/promptfoo
tools.what: A declarative, config-driven CLI for testing prompts and agents against a case set, comparing several models’ outputs, and red-teaming for vulnerabilities, closer to what a CI pipeline would call a test runner than a dashboard-first observability platform.

tools.name: wandb/weave
tools.what: Weights & Biases’ toolkit for tracing and evaluating LLM applications, built on the same company’s established experiment-tracking product for traditional ML training.

tools.name: agentic-community/mcp-gateway-registry
tools.what: An MCP gateway and registry: one governed address that agents discover MCP servers from once those servers are scattered.

tools.name: LangSmith Context Hub
tools.what: A hosted registry for the prompts and contexts an agent loads, versioned and environment-tagged.

tools.name: Microsoft Agent 365
tools.what: A hosted place to register and manage agents. Its vendor-neutrality is a claim reproduced here and not checked: nobody here has tested it against the product.

tools.name: mlflow/mlflow
tools.what: A server plus client libraries. Runs, parameters, artifacts and registered model versions go in; the registry half is what makes it a versioning surface rather than only a logging one.

tools.name: modelcontextprotocol/registry
tools.what: A registry service for MCP servers, developed by volunteers under the same GitHub organization that maintains the Model Context Protocol specification itself.

tools.name: Smithery
tools.what: A hosted directory of MCP servers plus a managed layer in front of them: the vendor states that it handles authentication, credentials and sessions on the adopting team’s behalf, so an agent can call a listed tool without that team standing up its own session/credential handling for that server.

tools.name: Claude Code plugin marketplaces
tools.what: A feature of Claude Code: a marketplace is a marketplace.json catalog, kept in a git repository or a local path, that lists plugins (skills, agents, hooks, MCP servers, LSP servers) for a team or a community to install from.

tools.name: Infisical/infisical
tools.what: A self-hosted service (with a managed tier) that holds secrets and brokers credentials on an outbound call, so the agent holds a placeholder and never the real value.
